thread.title: Robotics program blends versatility, creativity and hands-on creation
thread.title_full: Robotics program blends versatility, creativity and hands-on creation

author: silver state times
title: Robotics program blends versatility, creativity and hands-on creation
text:
The University of Nevada, Reno announced on Apr. 29 the launch of its new robotics master’s degree program and a robotics minor, aiming to prepare students for careers in robotics and automation. The master’s program began in fall 2025 and produced its first two graduates this past winter.
The university said these programs are designed to address the growing influence of robotics and artificial intelligence in society. Professor David Feil-Seifer leads the interdisciplinary effort, which draws from computer science, electrical engineering, and mechanical engineering.
“AI is changing the nature of the engineering workforce, and robotics is essentially physically embodied AI,” Computer Science & Engineering Professor David Feil-Seifer said. “And so, learning the skills that are needed to make these engineering problems actually work for real people in the real world, that’s what robotics does.”
Behnoush Hatami, one of the first graduates from the master’s program who is now pursuing a Ph.D., said: “I always was interested in robotics because it is an interdisciplinary field. It has computer vision, it has AI, it has programming and it has physical systems.”
Another graduate student, Denielle Oliva—who earned her bachelor’s degree at Nevada before completing her master’s last fall—said: “I like building something and seeing it work. I can do software, but with software there isn’t a tangible product that you’re holding afterwards. In robotics you program it; you build it.”
Heather Amistani echoed this sentiment about creativity within Feil-Seifer’s lab: “Creativity is a big thing for me, and in this lab I’m allowed to be creative,” she said. “That’s a big reason (to do robotics). We’re able to come up with different ideas and bounce them off each other and expand those ideas.”
Feil-Seifer added that anyone interested in applying technology to real-world problems could benefit from studying robotics: “Anything where engineering technology needs to meet the real world,” he said. “That’s what robotics provides the skills for.”
Faculty research areas include socially assistive robots (Feil-Seifer), agricultural robots (Parikshit Maini), civil infrastructure inspection (Jim La), human-robot interaction (Monica Nicolescu), autonomous systems (Christos Papachristos), as well as contributions from Sesh Commuri, Hao Xu, Floris van Breugel, and Yantao Shen across several departments.
The master’s degree accepts applicants with backgrounds in engineering or science who have completed coursework equivalent to an engineering minor. The minor is open to all Nevada Engineering students.
Oliva encouraged more students to consider joining: “I think a lot of people might be like [intimidated] going into a robotics minor but honestly the classes are super foundational… so I don’t think people should shy away from trying it.”
